guardianfootball.title: João Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flat
guardianfootball.description: There was a comic-strip feel to another eventful evening in the kingdom of Cristiano Ronaldo. Where to start? It was the 67th minute when his No 7 went up on the fourth official’s board, the cue to remove the captain’s armband from his left bicep before departing to a universal ovation, but for the pocket of Wales supporters. The referee, Donatas Rumsas, hurried him off the pitch but Ronaldo, his hair glazed copper, was presumably ruminating on a series of missed chances, a sitter from a few yards at the start of the second half, and his disallowed goal, after skating offside to latch on to a Bruno Fernandes pass. The grandiose “Siu” celebration went to waste, though try telling that to…

guardianfootball.title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’
guardianfootball.description: Two years ago the Brazilian thought his time at Barcelona was ending but, two La Liga titles later, he is now captain and the most potent No 9 in Europe For once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. In Barcelona or anywhere.…

guardianfootball.title: Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against Germany
guardianfootball.description: At least Germany can be sure it will not be dull. Jürgen Klopp had predicted his debut as head coach could be wild, a trait he would accept as long as his team were lively enough. Both transpired in a frayed, pinball-like game whose lack of quality could be forgiven on account of its entertainment levels. The Netherlands more than merited a brilliant late equaliser from Cody Gakpo and by the time those present had drawn breath it felt appropriate that, for all the talk of new dawns, everyone finished back where they had started. World domination is a far-off prospect for both of these flailing giants on such scrappy, frenetic evidence. But at least those with a stake in this famous old…

I have had good ideas and the odd great one that didn’t make it to air (attention the full-size unreferenced post-Keys and Gray elephant in the Soccer AM studio). I’ve had more awful ones. The updated release will take in 16 bonus tracks, including alternate versions, rare B-sides, BBC radio sessions, and live material from the Harmacy era. The original album has also been remastered for the reissue. It will be made available on CD, vinyl and digital formats. Harmacy was Sebadoh's breakout sixth album, and found them sitting at a crossroads in their sound between harder slacker rock and gentler tones. Listen to an alternate version of 'Beauty Of The Ride', lifted from the reissue, below. Sub Pop will release Harmacy (30th…

quietus.description: Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording captures the D.C. punk group's recording session at Arlington, Virginia’s Inner Ear Studios Bad Brains are releasing their fabled first demo tape recording for the first time, in the form of Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording (Inner Ear - March 1979). In a statement, Bad Brains bassist Darryl Jenifer said: "The riff for ‘Pay To Cum’ started as a stream of punk rock vibes fueled by The Ramones, The Damned, and Return To Forever. It was a gift that served as a…

quietus.title: Erol Alkan Details Book on Club Night Trash
quietus.description: Marking 20 years since the final edition of the party, the book will look back over its decade-long run Erol Alkan is writing a book on Trash, the legendary London club night that he founded in 1997. Trash: A Club, A Sound, A Home comes 30 years on from the event's founding, and two decades on from its final edition, and will look back over the decade-long history of the party, as well as the scene that thrived around it as electronic and guitar music cross-pollinated. Trash's original run as a Monday party at London venues like Plastic People and The End helped to break down various genre boundaries as music scenes such as electroclash, nu-rave and blog house emerged. The club night...

quietus.title: Brain Damage: 1991 and how Grunge Forced Metal to Grow up
quietus.description: 1991 was the most pivotal year of rock's history thanks to Nirvana, Metallica and Red Hot Chili Peppers, but the closer you look the more complex the story gets, says Joel McIver I’ve just read Shooting Up And Making Out, the imminent memoir by the late L7 bassist Jennifer Finch, a great book that among many other insights tells us exactly what it was like to be a maker of abrasive, semi-underground guitar music in the specific locales of Los Angeles and Seattle in the late 80s. It’s full of vivid anecdotes, one of which is Finch’s account of working in a strip joint in Hollywood in the mid-80s, needing to survive as a semi-homeless punk kid with an ingrained heroin...

quietus.title: 35 Years On: A Tribe Called Quest’s The Low End Theory Revisited
quietus.description: Angus Batey revisits the history and lasting legacy of A Tribe Called Quest's Low End Theory There's a wonderful moment in Beats, Rhymes and Life: The Travels of A Tribe Called Quest, Michael Rapaport's fascinating documentary about A Tribe Called Quest. Jive records CEO Barry Weiss recalls the label's internal reaction when staff first heard the group's second LP, The Low End Theory. "It was very different to the first album," Weiss tells Rapaport. "It wasn't as 'left' in some ways, and we were concerned that maybe it was gonna miss the mark - that maybe they were trying to go too commercial, that it didn't have the artistic integrity that [the debut] People's Instinctive Travels [In the…

quietus.title: Shared Frequency: Quiet Storm by Space Afrika
quietus.description: Manchester duo go big, vastly expanding their palette with strings, harps and a plethora of special guests Photograph credit: Timon Benson. Art Direction: Alexander Luc and Timon Benson. Clothing: Omar Afridi X VUJA DÉ There is a particular kind of light that only exists after rain has finished falling but before the sun has arrived – a grey-gold hour where the wet ground holds more colour than the sky. Space Afrika has always made records that live inside that hour. Honest Labour, the pair's breakout 2021 statement, was full of it: shortwave murmur, tower-block wind, the feeling of being simultaneously inside a crowd and entirely alone. Five years on, Joshua Tarelle Reid and Joshua Inyang…

quietus.title: Immersion – What Is Lost Will Return
quietus.description: Immersion What Is Lost Will Return Immersion find new shapes within familiar sounds, turning repetition into something restless What Is Lost Will Return by Immersion Given the history behind Immersion, it would be easy to hear What Is Lost Will Return as a record looking backwards. That is a useful quality for a band with Colin Newman and Malka Spigel’s respective histories: there is no shortage of past to draw upon. But What Is Lost Will Return feels pleasingly unconcerned with doing so. It occupies a strange, immediate space somewhere between song, groove and electronic abstraction, where guitars, bass, electronics and voices seem to be continually finding new combinations. ‘Nephology’…

quietus.title: Richard Skelton and Lawrence English Reveal Collaborative LP, ‘NOON’
quietus.description: The four-track release is out in November Richard Skelton and Lawrence English have teamed up for their first collaborative LP together, titled NOON. Comprised of four long-form tracks, the project came about from conversations that the two artists, on opposite sides of the world, had in 2021 about the volatile environments that they found themselves in, as Australia experience flooding and extreme weather, and Ireland's Atlantic coastline was hit by storms. In a joint statement, Skeleton and English said: “NOON operates as a palindrome of listening practices and experimentation, and moreover as a shared temporal marker that reminds us of the vastly finite turnings of our world." Watch a…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Dungen :: Vidrig Vår
aquariumdrunkard.description: On the veteran Swedish outfit's most pared down and elegant affair, Vidrig Vår showcases Dungen still operating on a psychedelic wavelength not found elsewhere. Built around bandleader Gustav Ejste's panoramic piano progressions, the ballad-centric record flows with the weightless springtime atmosphere of the band's organically cinematic orbit.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Asher White :: Love Aggregates
aquariumdrunkard.description: Asher White goes maximalist on Love Aggregates , building heavy doses of orchestral power pop from her bedroom. A fragmentary heartbreak album touching on dysphoria, precarious labor, Jerry Garcia, Citi Bikes, and Flatbush in the snow, it transforms intimate falsettos, arpeggiating guitars, and toy piano melodies into a luminous, redemptive vision of love.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Those Were the Days of Miracle and Wonder :: Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40
aquariumdrunkard.description: Paul Simon’s 1986 album Graceland exists in this weird state, an album that eternally evokes 1986, but always sounds so different from other albums of its era. It’s an collection that’s self absorbed, but also so relatable when the listener finds themselves hitting middle age. It brought world music to the forefront, but also presented a misleading picture. It’s a fascinating study in contrast and now, some 40 years later it’s an album we still can’t make up our minds about even as we listen to it for the hundredth time.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Aquarium Drunkard Show: SIRIUS/XMU (7pm PDT, Channel 35)
aquariumdrunkard.description: Broadcasting from northeast Los Angeles — the Aquarium Drunkard Show on SIRIUS/XMU, channel 35. 7pm California time, Wednesdays. Subterranean nocturnes dissolve into the horizon. Somewhere between Tokyo, NYC, Caracas and outer space—electric jazz, Japanese fusion, polyrhythms, Rio groove, cosmic funk, library exotica and studio alchemy. 34.1090° N, 118.2334° W

aquariumdrunkard.title: Love :: Four Sail
aquariumdrunkard.description: For many, Forever Changes is where the Love story ends. Whether viewed as a retooled evolution of the band or simply that of Arthur Lee, Four Sail is an essential part of the Love discography. With a driving edge partly recalling the proto-punk energy of Da Capo with the modern hard rock zeitgeist of 1969, Lee's superb new lineup delivers the intentions behind "combining the east and west coast sounds with the European sounds, plus a few of my own ideas".

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Matt Baldwin
aquariumdrunkard.description: This week on the show, guitarist and psychotherapist Matt Baldwin, who is here to teach you How To Play Guitar. OK, not exactly. But Baldwin is the author of ⁠How To Play Guitar⁠, a series of zines that have been collected into a handsome book edition. If you’re just picking up the instrument, well, Baldwin isn’t writing about how to play a C chord or run scales. These aren’t “how to” guides so much as “why to” prompts, stressing intuition over technique, dismissal of music industry norms, and the imperative to hone a singular, personal philosophy regarding the instrument—think Captain Beefheart’s “Ten Commandments of Playing Guitar.” In this talk, we discuss his own guitar journey, the…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts :: Second Song
aquariumdrunkard.description: At 80, Neil Young remains gloriously unfinished. Second Song , his latest with the Chrome Hearts, is a weathered, luminous meditation on memory, mortality, love, and the strange passage of time. With shimmering textures, warm harmonies, wandering tempos, and that unmistakably vulnerable voice, Young looks backward without quite letting go of the future. An elegiac, deeply human record from an artist still searching for the song.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Índio da Cuíca :: Zing Zing
aquariumdrunkard.description: At 70, Brazilian percussionist Índio da Cuíca reinvented himself as one of the country’s strangest musical voices. His cuíca—usually a squeaky rhythmic accent—is transformed into a melodic instrument of uncanny virtuosity, set against samba, capoeira, Afro-Brazilian spirituals and warped pop forms. On Zing Zing , that “avant-traditional” vision expands further, as cavaquinho, pandeiro, berimbau and bandolim collide with guitars, synths and samples. Samba music from some parallel universe.

Sometimes those changes are organic, a gradual movement that is driven by the changing needs of speakers. But sometimes those changes are engineered from above, to serve the needs of those in power. After years of algorithmic censorship, we now see words like “unalive” or “le$bean” replacing their antecedents even in conversation, even if only ironically. (As if to prove the point, the plot of the new film by Denis Côté, Nobody’s Violence , manages to hinge on the issue of assisted suicide without ever uttering the s-word. Clockwise from top-left: The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011), Merantau (Gareth Evans, 2009), The Raid 2 (Gareth Evans, 2014), The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011). It needs virtually no introduction. Fifteen years after its world premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the 2011 Toronto International Film Festival, The Raid (2011) has so shaped the landscape of contemporary action cinema that it’s birthed its own prepositional descriptor: “like The Raid ” adorns sundry headlines to describe any action film featuring some combination of a single-location setting, gritty atmosphere, barbarous…

As in our sleeping dreams, a sense of infinite possibility stretches before us. That seemingly limitless vista soon disappoints once it is foreshortened into something real and recognizable, such as a place, an environment, a mood, a character, a theme, a genre, or a plot. Yet without these comfortable anchors, something that resembles prenatal bliss envelops our ignorance, and the fact that we can imagine almost anything makes the start of…

Once used as a checkpoint for Holy Land pilgrims, and then—after the plague reached the lagoon in 1423—a leper colony, it is, in 2026 AD, now home to the virtual reality sidebar. The architecture has barely changed through the centuries. Dotting the high-ceilinged corridors that used to house the city’s moribund, festival guests can find various booths, each promising…
